default.q.1200_moji_n3-t48-q1.explanation: The adverb「今ごろ」(今頃) means “around this time” or “at about this time of year.” Speakers use it when imagining or guessing that something is happening elsewhere, so it often appears with conjectural endings such as「～だろう / ～でしょう」or「～はずだ」. In context, sentence (b) means: "Around this time, the cherry blossoms in Tokyo are probably in full bloom, aren’t they?" A typical example is: 「田中さんは今ごろ、家でゆっくり休んでいるはずだ。」(By this time, Tanaka must be relaxing at home.) To avoid this trap, distinguish「今から」(from now on),「今にも」(about to happen, used with ～そう), and「このごろ」(these days, referring to recent habits or trends) from「今ごろ」(a conjecture about a point in time).
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t48-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) To announce that an action will begin immediately after speaking, use 「今から」or「これから」, not 「今ごろ」.

default.q.1200_moji_n3-t48-q10.explanation: The verb 「増やす」（ふやす）is a Group 1 transitive verb (他動詞) meaning to intentionally increase the quantity, volume, or scale of something. It normally takes the object marker を in the pattern 「〜を増やす」. In sentence (c), the speaker uses the negative 「〜ないで」 (do not do V; instead do something else) to give advice: “Don’t increase the number of people; improve work efficiency instead.” The key distinction between the easily confused pair 「増える - 増やす」 is the particle: when the subject marked by 「が」 changes in quantity or number on its own, use the intransitive verb 「増える」, as in sentences (b) and (d); when an agent intentionally increases something marked by 「を」, use the transitive verb 「増やす」. In sentence (a), nouns expressing an abstract degree or natural phenomenon, such as 「暑さ」 (heat), are not normally combined with 「増やす」 or 「増える」. Japanese uses 「増す」 (ます) instead. Another example is: 「健康のために、毎日野菜を食べる量を増やしています。」 (For my health, I am increasing the amount of vegetables I eat every day.)

The complete sentence in (d) means: "The fugitive had been hiding for about three years, but was finally caught." To avoid the traps in (a) and (b), remember that つかまえる is not used for stolen objects such as a wallet or bicycle; use 盗まれる instead. It also does not mean picking plants, for which 摘む is used. default.q.1200_moji_n3-t48-q13.explanation: The adverb 「せめて」means “at least” or “at the very least”. It has a strong emotional nuance and commonly occurs with expressions of desire, requests, or regret, such as 「～たい」, 「～てほしい」, 「～てください」, and 「～ばいいのに」. The sentence means: “Since you went all the way to near here, wouldn’t it have been nice if you had taken at least a little time to call me?” For comparison: 「忙しくても、せめて日曜日くらいはゆっくり休みたい。」 (“Even when I am busy, I want to be able to relax at least on Sundays.”) Unlike 「少なくとも」 and 「せいぜい」, which are used for objective estimates or quantities, 「せめて」must be connected to the speaker’s desire or longing.

The verb 比べる (to compare) combines with に and と to form the comparison pattern「〜に比べると」(compared with ~). It is appropriate for comparing the safety of Tokyo and New York.

In the N3 exam, these similar-sounding verbs are easy to confuse, so remember: 「比べる - くらべる」 (compare), 「並べる - ならべる」 (arrange or line up, as in sentence b), and 「調べる - しらべる」 (look up or investigate, as in sentence c).

default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) To describe arranging dishes attractively on a table, the correct word is 並べる (“arrange” or “line up”), not 比べる.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) To ask someone to look up or check how long it takes to reach the next station, use the verb 調べる (to look up or check), not 比べる (to compare).

Therefore, the complete sentence means: “Because I have not yet gotten used to traveling by boat, my legs keep wobbling and I cannot stand steadily.” A similar everyday example is: 「熱が高くて頭がふらふらする。」(I have a high fever, so I feel dizzy.) An important JLPT distinction is 「ふらふら」(swaying or staggering from weakness/dizziness) versus the easily confused 「ぶらぶら」(wandering around casually or idly, as in choice (c)).

default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) Irritation and impatience when the other person is slow to respond are expressed with an onomatopoeic word such as 「いらいら」, not 「ふらふら」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) To describe losing one's job and then staying at home, idling around with nothing to do, the appropriate word is 「ぶらぶら」 or 「ごろごろ」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q3.why.3: ✗ (d) To describe being unable to hold back and letting out a giggle or snort of laughter, use 「くすくす」or 「ぷっと」, not 「ふらふら」.

The verb 「倒れる」(たおれる) means “to fall” or “to topple,” and is the most appropriate choice for a vertical object such as a tree being knocked down by an external force.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q4.explanation: The intransitive verb 「倒れる」（たおれる—Group 2）has the core meaning "to fall, topple, or collapse." It is used when something that was originally upright, such as a tree, utility pole, or building, loses its balance due to an external force and falls, or when a person collapses from exhaustion. In sentence (b), the dictionary form combines with the N3 grammar pattern 「V-る + ことなく」, which has a formal nuance meaning "without ..." or "never ..." The complete translation is: "Despite being hit by strong winds, the ancient pine tree remained standing proudly without toppling." To answer this type of question, distinguish 「倒れる」 from 「壊れる」, used for objects breaking or malfunctioning, such as the camera in sentence (c), and 「疲れる」, which means to become tired, as in sentence (a). Remember that 「倒れる」 involves a change in posture from "standing" to "lying or fallen." For comparison: 昨夜の台風で、庭の大きな木が倒れてしまった。(The typhoon last night knocked down the large tree in the garden.)
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) To express being exhausted and needing rest, 「疲れた」is used, not 「倒れた」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q4.why.1: ✓ (b) 「倒れる」 describes trees losing their balance and falling over in a storm, making it an entirely accurate semantic combination.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) If a camera falls and breaks into pieces, 「壊れて」or「割れて」must be used; 「倒れて」cannot be used.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) To describe flowers blooming abundantly everywhere, Japanese uses expressions such as「咲き乱れる」or「​​あふれる」, not「倒れる」.

「割れる」 is an intransitive verb describing fragile objects such as glass or pottery cracking and breaking into pieces. It naturally modifies 「音」 in 「ガラスの割れる音」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q5.explanation: The intransitive group 2 verb 「割れる」(われる) means to crack or shatter into pieces. It is used for hard but brittle objects such as glass (ガラス), ceramics (皿, コップ), and eggshells (卵). In sentence (d), the dictionary form 「割れる」directly modifies the noun 「音」, producing the sentence: “The strong wind blew the window open, accompanied by the sound of breaking glass.” At N3 level, remember that 「割れる」cannot take the particle 「を」; choice c would require the transitive verb 「割る」. Also distinguish it from 「破れる」, used for paper or bags that tear in choice b, and 「壊れる」, used for machines that break down in choice a. Example: 「不注意でテーブルから落ちたグラスが割れてしまった。」(The glass fell from the table due to carelessness and shattered.)
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) For a machine malfunctioning or breaking down, use 「壊れる」 or 「壊す」, not 「割れる」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q5.why.1: ✗ (b) Soft objects such as packaging or bags that tear must be used with the verb「破れる」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) 「割れる」is an intransitive verb, so it cannot be used with the particle「を」. To express breaking a plate, use the transitive verb「割る」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q5.why.3: ✓ (d) 「割れる」combines correctly with the noun 「ガラス」for glass and is in the dictionary form to modify 「音」.

The verb 切れる naturally combines with 期限 in the fixed expression「期限が切れる」, meaning that something expires or its period of validity ends.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q6.explanation: The verb 切れる (きれる) is a Group 2 intransitive verb. Besides its physical meanings “be cut” or “tear,” it combines with が and nouns referring to time limits or energy—such as 期限, 電池, and 息—to express something expiring, running out, or naturally losing effect. In this context, the complete sentence means: "This multi-ride ticket booklet will expire on March 31." For comparison: 「パスポートの有効期限が切れてしまったので、更新に行きます。」 (My passport has expired, so I am going to renew it.) Distinguish the intransitive verb 切れる, often used with が when something expires or breaks on its own, from the transitive verb 切る, which describes actively cutting something and takes を, as in choice (b). Also do not confuse it with 消える, used when a light or fire goes out, or 折れる, used when a slender object bends or breaks.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q6.why.0: ✓ (a) The fixed expression 「期限が切れる」is used precisely to mean that the validity period has ended or something has expired.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) The intentional action of cutting food into small pieces requires the transitive verb 切る in the te-form, 切って, not the intransitive verb 切れる.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) To describe a signal light going out, use the verb 消える rather than 切れる.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q6.why.3: ✗ (d) To describe a long, thin object such as a pen snapping with a “crack” after being stepped on, the verb 折れる must be used instead of 切れる.

It commonly appears in the structure 「V-る / V-ない + ように祈る（祈っています）」. Sentence (b) means: “I sincerely pray that my wish will soon come true.” Distinguish it from sentence (a): 「祈る」expresses a personal wish or prayer and is never used to ask or order someone else to act, as in 「〜ように頼む」. The verb 「ぬれる」（濡れる）means to become wet or get soaked, and naturally combines with 「雨にぬれる」to describe getting wet in the rain.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q8.explanation: 「ぬれる」（濡れる） is a group 2 intransitive verb describing a person or object becoming wet after coming into contact with water or another liquid. It commonly takes the particle に in the pattern 「[liquid] にぬれる」. The complete meaning of sentence (d) is: “I got soaked by the rain and caught a cold.” Compare it with this common example: 「雨宿りをしたので、服はぬれずに済んだ。」(Because I took shelter from the rain, my clothes stayed dry.) To avoid being misled in the test, distinguish 「ぬれる」 from similar-sounding verbs such as 「ふれる」(触れる – touch, come into contact with) and 「かれる」(枯れる – wither). The key rule is that 「ぬれる」 must involve becoming wet.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q8.why.0: ✗ (a) To describe plants becoming dry and withered in winter, the correct word is 「枯れる」(かれる), not 「ぬれる」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) For the sun sinking below the horizon, the verb 「沈む」（しずむ）must be used, not 「ぬれる」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q8.why.2: ✗ (c) When an object comes into direct contact with air and changes color, the correct word is 「触れる」（ふれる）.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q8.why.3: ✓ (d) 「雨にぬれる」is the standard collocation meaning “get caught in the rain” or “get wet from the rain,” which fits perfectly with the resulting cold.

「試合」 specifically refers to a competitive sporting match between two sides, so 「サッカーの試合」 is the correct collocation.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q9.explanation: The noun 「試合」(しあい) means "match" or "game". It is used when two individuals or teams compete directly under established rules in a sport such as soccer, basketball, tennis, or martial arts to determine a winner. Combined with 「～のが楽しみです」(to look forward to doing something), the complete sentence means: "I am really looking forward to watching the soccer match after the exam period ends." Similar example: 「明日、テニスの試合に出場する予定です」(I plan to compete in a tennis match tomorrow.) An important N3 distinction is: 「試合」is used for direct athletic competition, 「競争」(as in 価格競争) for competition involving speed or the marketplace, and 「コンクール」for contests showcasing artistic talent.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) The 100-meter race is a sport that measures speed by time, so 「競争」or 「レース」must be used instead of 「試合」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q9.why.1: ✓ (b) サッカー is a sport played competitively between two teams, so combining it with 「試合」 is completely correct.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) Price competition in economics is expressed by the fixed phrase 「価格競争」, not 「価格試合」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t52-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) A performance competition, such as a piano competition, should use 「コンクール」 or 「コンテスト」 rather than 「試合」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 明日は（きっと）晴れるでしょう。
The adverb「きっと」expresses a highly confident personal prediction or assumption. It naturally combines with the conjectural sentence ending「〜でしょう」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q1.explanation: The adverb 「きっと」 expresses a subjective prediction or expectation held with a high degree of confidence (around 80–90%). It commonly occurs with speculative sentence endings such as 「〜でしょう」, 「〜だろう」, and 「〜に違いない」. The complete test sentence means: “The weather will surely be nice tomorrow, won’t it?” For encouragement, consider: 「彼ならきっと合格できるよ。」(He can definitely pass.) An important JLPT distinction is that 「きっと」 differs from 「必ず」, which expresses inevitability, an established rule, or an obligation, and 「ぜひ」, which expresses a strong desire or an earnest invitation. Do not use 「きっと」 for requests or scientific facts.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) 「きっと」is not used in direct requests such as「〜てください」; in this case, 「必ず」should be used.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「きっと」is not used for invitations or polite recommendations; in this context, use「ぜひ」or「どうぞ」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「きっと」 is used only for subjective conjecture, not for natural laws or obvious objective facts (when making a much stronger comparison, use 「ずっと」).
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) 「きっと」correctly combines with the conjectural pattern 「〜でしょう」to express the speaker’s highly confident supposition.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) ６月は一年のうちで、（とくに）雨の多い時期です。
The adverb とくに (特に) means “especially” or “in particular.” It highlights something with an outstanding characteristic within a defined range, here June within the year.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q10.explanation: The adverb とくに (特に, especially, particularly) highlights a person, thing, phenomenon, or time as standing out from others in the same group. It often appears in comparison-range structures such as 「～の中で／のうちで、特に…」 or before an adjective or verb to emphasize degree. In sentence (c), combining 「一年のうちで」 (within a year) with 「とくに雨の多い時期」 (a period with particularly heavy rainfall) creates the meaning: “Of the entire year, June is the period with especially frequent rain.” Example: 「果物は何でも好きですが、特にりんごが好きです。」 (I like all kinds of fruit, but I especially like apples.) Be careful with sentence (d): when used with the negative, 特に～ない means “nothing in particular,” as in 「特に用事はない」, unlike まったく or ぜんぜん, which strongly emphasize complete negation.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) The adverb とくに cannot directly modify the action 買いました by itself when no notable comparison or scope has been established.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q10.why.1: ✗ (b) This is incorrect because とくに is an adverb and cannot follow の to modify the noun 会議. This context requires an expression of substitution such as 代わりに.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q10.why.2: ✓ (c) とくにis used correctly to emphasize the month with exceptionally high rainfall (June) within the year as a whole (一年のうちで).
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) This is incorrect because when expressing that something was completely incomprehensible despite trying, Japanese uses まったく or ぜんぜん, not とくに.

The adverb 「なるべく」 means “as much as possible” or “to the extent possible,” fitting the pattern 「〜ようにしている」, which expresses a personal habit or effort.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q11.explanation: The adverb「なるべく」(synonymous with「できるだけ」) means “as much as possible within the circumstances” and commonly occurs with expressions of personal intention or effort, such as「〜ようにする」and「〜たい」, as well as polite requests like「〜てください」. In context (d), the complete sentence means: “I always try to limit my alcohol consumption as much as possible.” Another practical example is:「なるべく早く返事をください。」(Please reply as soon as possible.) To distinguish it from similar adverbs, remember that「なるべく」expresses flexible effort. It does not combine with absolute obligation such as「〜なければならない」(b, which requires「必ず」), inference or expectation (a, which requires「きっと」), or a negative quantity limit with「〜しか」(c, which requires「せいぜい」).
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q11.why.0: ✗ (a) 「なるべく」 is not used for an objective prediction or conjecture such as 「〜でしょう」; the adverb 「きっと」 is appropriate here.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) 「なるべく」(as much as possible) conflicts with an expression of absolute obligation such as「〜なければならない」. This sentence requires「必ず」or「絶対に」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q11.why.2: ✗ (c) 「なるべく」is not used with a quantity limit and the negative pattern 「〜しか...ない」. This case requires an adverb expressing a maximum, such as 「せいぜい」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q11.why.3: ✓ (d) 「なるべく」combines correctly with the effort structure「〜ようにしている」to express consciously trying to do something as much as possible within one's ability.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q12.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 海外旅行の（たびに）、その国のお土産を買って帰ります。
The structure 「N のたびに」 expresses a repeated pattern: whenever event A occurs, action B is also carried out.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q12.explanation: The grammar pattern 「〜たびに」 combines with the dictionary form of a verb (V-る) or a noun followed by 「の」 (N の) and means "every time..." It emphasizes a regular, repeated relationship between events. It does not combine with the negative form 「V-ない」 or past form 「V-た」, and the following clause should not describe a random one-time event. Sentence (c) is correct and means: "Every time I travel abroad, I buy a souvenir from that country and bring it home." Another example is 「この写真を見るたびに、楽しかった旅行を思い出します。」 (Every time I look at this photograph, I remember that enjoyable trip.) Use 「〜ないうちに」 when advising someone to act before a condition changes, as in (a), and use 「〜たら / 〜とたん」 rather than 「たびに」 for sudden natural events that occurred in the past, as in (d).
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q12.why.0: ✗ (a) The grammar pattern 「たびに」 cannot be used with the negative form 「V-ない」. In this context, 「うちに」 is required: 「冷めないうちに」 (“while it is still hot”).
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q12.why.1: ✗ (b) 「たびに」expresses a repeated habit or rule, so the following clause cannot end with the simple past 「忘れた」referring to one occurrence; it should use 「忘れてしまう」or 「忘れる」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q12.why.2: ✓ (c) The structure 「N のたびに」is used correctly with the following clause to express an action that is repeated every time the speaker travels abroad.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q12.why.3: ✗ (d) This is incorrect because 「たびに」does not combine with the past form 「V-た」, and it is not used for a random, unexpected one-time event such as rain suddenly starting.

The interjection 「おや」 expresses surprise or the sudden realization of something unexpected, fitting the context of being startled to notice that it is already noon.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q13.explanation: 「おや」 is an interjection usually placed at the beginning of a sentence. It expresses mild surprise or bewilderment when the speaker suddenly notices something unexpected, similar to “Oh?” or “Well, look at that.” The complete sentence means: “Oh, it’s already twelve o’clock?” Another example is: 「おや、雨が降ってきた。」(Oh, it’s started raining.) Remember that 「おや」 expresses the speaker’s own surprise at a discovery, unlike 「ほら」, which calls another person’s attention to something, or the panicked reaction used in sentence (d).
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q13.why.0: ✗ (a) To direct the listener's attention to a specific object, as in this sentence, Japanese uses the interjection 「ほら」, not 「おや」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q13.why.1: ✓ (b) 「おや」is used correctly to express mild surprise when the speaker suddenly realizes that it is already midnight.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q13.why.2: ✗ (c) This is an expression of concern and understanding toward the other person’s hardships; it is not used with the exclamation of surprise 「おや」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q13.why.3: ✗ (d) 「おや」expresses mild surprise and is not appropriate in a panicked or dangerous situation such as one involving「大変だ」.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q14.verdict:

「これ以上」 combined with a negative predicate indicates that the limit has been reached, meaning that nothing more needs to or can be done.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q14.explanation: The expression 「これ以上」 commonly occurs with a negative predicate to define the absolute limit of a degree or quantity, conveying the sense that “any more than this is impossible or unnecessary.” Based on this structure, the complete sentence means: “At the current level, there is nothing left that needs to be revised.” A familiar example is:「これ以上待つことはできません」(I can’t wait any longer). N3 learners should clearly distinguish the distractors: choice b uses 「その上」 to add information (“in addition”); choice c uses 「～上で」 to indicate the context in which an action is performed (“when doing…”); 「～以上（は）」 means “once…” or “now that…” and never combines with 「で」; and choice d uses 「～以来」 for an action or state continuing from a point in the past.

「ずいぶん」 functions as an adverb of high degree (“very much,” “considerably”) and naturally combines with 「違っている」 to express a substantial difference from the comparison point.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q2.explanation: 「ずいぶん」（随分）is an adverb of degree meaning "quite," "very," or "considerably." It is commonly used when the speaker notices that a state or change has exceeded the normal level or initial expectations. It mainly combines with adjectives or verbs expressing change or difference, such as 違う and 変わる, in affirmative sentences. Therefore, sentence (c) means: "The market today is considerably different from what it was 10 years ago." Another example is:「久しぶりに会った彼は、背がずいぶん伸びていた。」(When I saw him again after a long time, he had grown considerably taller.) default.q.1200_moji_n3-t53-q2.why.2: ✓ (c) Correct because the adverb 「ずいぶん」 combines naturally with the affirmative predicate 「違っている」 to emphasize that the difference is very large after a long period of time。

Choice (c) therefore means: “If you keep going straight along this road, you will reach the end of it.” Another example is: この道をずっと進むと、右手に大きな公園が見えます (If you keep going straight along this road, you will see a large park on your right). The kanji word 「見事」 has the special kun-reading 「みごと」 and is used to praise an excellent result or remarkable achievement.
default.q.1200_moji_n3-t9-q9.explanation: 「見事」 is originally a na-adjective expressing admiration for a complete achievement that exceeds expectations. When combined with に as 「見事に + V」, it functions as an adverb modifying the following action. In the test sentence, 「彼は合格率５%の試験を受けて、（見事）に合格した。」 means: "He took an exam with a pass rate of only 5% and passed with flying colors." A similar example is 「厳しい練習の末、彼女は見事に優勝を果たした。」 (After rigorous training, she won the championship brilliantly.) A common trap is to read the compound as 「けんじ」 based on familiar on-readings. Remember that 「見事」 is a special native reading: 見 is read 「み」 and 事 changes from こと to 「ごと」.
